The main question of the project: when more of demand is met by wind and solar,
how much lower is the price, and does that effect change over time?

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| code-summary: "Code: load packages and data"

library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)

# Run the scripts in R/ first (see the README).
ercot <- read_rds(here::here("data/processed/ercot_hourly.rds"))
```

```{r}
#| label: prep
#| code-summary: "Code: prepare modeling data"

base <- ercot |>
  filter(hub == "HB_BUSAVG", !is.na(renewable_share)) |>
  mutate(
    hour_f  = factor(hour_local),
    month_f = factor(month(time_local)),
    year_f  = factor(year),
    uri     = time_local >= as.POSIXct("2021-02-10", tz = "America/Chicago") &
              time_local <  as.POSIXct("2021-02-21", tz = "America/Chicago"),
    season  = case_when(month(time_local) %in% 6:8        ~ "Summer",
                        month(time_local) %in% c(12, 1, 2) ~ "Winter",
                        TRUE                               ~ "Spring/Fall")
  )

no_uri <- filter(base, !uri)

# Effect of renewables on price, per 10 percentage points of renewable share
effect <- function(model) {
  tibble(
    effect_per_10pp = coef(model)[["renewable_share"]] * 0.1,
    std_error       = sqrt(diag(vcov(model)))[["renewable_share"]] * 0.1,
    r_squared       = summary(model)$r.squared,
    hours           = nobs(model)
  )
}
```

## Look first

### Price vs. renewable share

```{r}
#| label: look-share
#| code-summary: "Code: median price by renewable share"

no_uri |>
  mutate(share_bin = cut(renewable_share, breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.1),
                         labels = paste0(seq(0, 90, 10), "–", seq(10, 100, 10), "%"))) |>
  filter(!is.na(share_bin)) |>
  group_by(share_bin) |>
  summarise(median_price = median(rt_price), hours = n()) |>
  filter(hours >= 50) |>
  ggplot(aes(share_bin, median_price)) +
  geom_col(fill = "seagreen") +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("$", round(median_price))), vjust = -0.4) +
  geom_text(aes(y = 0, label = paste(scales::comma(hours), "hrs")),
            vjust = 1.5, size = 3, colour = "grey30") +
  labs(x = "Share of demand met by wind + solar",
       y = "Typical (median) price, $/MWh",
       title = "The more wind and solar, the cheaper the power")
```
*How to read: each bar groups hours by how much of demand wind and solar
covered. Bar height is the typical price in those hours; the number below each
bar is how many hours fall in that group.*

**Findings:** As wind and solar supply more of demand, power gets cheaper. In
hours when they cover 10–20% of demand, the typical price is about \$41/MWh;
when they cover 50–60%, it falls to about \$15/MWh. This shows that renewables
and lower prices go together; the Model section tests whether renewables are
the cause.

### Price vs. net load

Net load is demand minus wind and solar: the power that gas, coal and nuclear
plants still have to supply.

```{r}
#| label: look-net-load
#| code-summary: "Code: median price by net load"

no_uri |>
  mutate(net_load_bin = cut(net_load_mw / 1000, breaks = seq(10, 70, 5),
                            labels = paste0(seq(10, 65, 5), "–", seq(15, 70, 5)))) |>
  filter(!is.na(net_load_bin)) |>
  group_by(net_load_bin) |>
  summarise(median_price = median(rt_price), hours = n()) |>
  filter(hours >= 50) |>
  ggplot(aes(net_load_bin, median_price)) +
  geom_col(fill = "firebrick") +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("$", round(median_price))), vjust = -0.4) +
  geom_text(aes(y = 0, label = paste(scales::comma(hours), "hrs")),
            vjust = 1.5, size = 3, colour = "grey30") +
  labs(x = "Net load (thousand MW): the demand wind and solar don't cover",
       y = "Typical (median) price, $/MWh",
       title = "Prices stay low until the other power plants are stretched, then climb")
```
*How to read: each bar groups hours by net load, in thousands of MW. Bar height
is the typical price in those hours.*

**Findings:** Prices stay low across most net load levels, then rise sharply
once net load passes about 60,000 MW. In the rare hours above 65,000 MW
(129 hours), the typical price is about \$488/MWh, more than ten times the
usual price of about \$41. The renewable share chart hides these spikes:
those heat-wave evenings are mixed in with thousands of cheap low-renewable
hours. Net load separates them, which makes it the better predictor of price.

## Model

### How much do renewables lower prices?

Each model adds one thing:

1. Renewable share alone.
2. Adds hour, month and year, so the comparison is between hours that are
   otherwise alike (same time of day, same season, same year).
3. Model 2 without Winter Storm Uri.
4. Model 3 using day-ahead instead of real-time prices.

```{r}
#| label: model-main
#| code-summary: "Code: regression models"

models <- list(
  "1. Renewable share only"             = lm(rt_price ~ renewable_share, base),
  "2. + hour, month, year controls"     = lm(rt_price ~ renewable_share + hour_f + month_f + year_f, base),
  "3. Model 2 without Winter Storm Uri" = lm(rt_price ~ renewable_share + hour_f + month_f + year_f, no_uri),
  "4. Model 3 with day-ahead price"     = lm(da_price ~ renewable_share + hour_f + month_f + year_f, no_uri)
)

map_dfr(models, effect, .id = "model") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = c(0, 2, 2, 3, 0),
               caption = "Change in price ($/MWh) for each 10-point rise in renewable share")
```

**Findings:** More wind and solar means lower prices. After comparing only
similar hours (same time of day, month and year) and removing Winter Storm Uri,
each 10-point increase in wind and solar's share of demand lowers the real-time
price by about \$12/MWh, and the day-ahead price by about \$9.50/MWh.

Including Uri more than triples the estimate (to about \$42), because that one
week combined very little wind and solar with \$9,000 prices. We use the
estimate without Uri, since a single extreme event shouldn't drive the result.

Renewable share explains only 6–10% of the hour-to-hour swings in price; most
of the variation comes from rare price spikes that depend on other things, such
as demand and power plant outages.

### Has the effect changed over time?

```{r}
#| label: model-by-year
#| code-summary: "Code: effect by year"

by_year <- no_uri |>
  group_by(year) |>
  group_modify(~ effect(lm(rt_price ~ renewable_share + hour_f + month_f, data = .x))) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(by_year, aes(factor(year), effect_per_10pp)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey40") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = effect_per_10pp - 1.96 * std_error,
                    ymax = effect_per_10pp + 1.96 * std_error), width = 0.2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("$", round(effect_per_10pp, 1))),
            vjust = ifelse(by_year$effect_per_10pp < 0, 1.8, -0.8), colour = "white") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Price change per 10-point rise in renewable share ($/MWh)",
       title = "Effect of renewables on price, by year")

knitr::kable(by_year, digits = c(0, 2, 2, 3, 0), caption = "Effect by year")
```

**Findings:** Renewables lowered prices in every year, by about \$10–13/MWh per
10-point increase, except in 2022, when the effect nearly doubled to about \$20.
2022 was a year of expensive natural gas, so every MWh of wind and solar
replaced costlier gas power and saved more. As gas got cheaper in 2023–2024,
the effect shrank back.

In 2025, renewables explain far more of the hour-to-hour price swings (23%,
up from 7–10% in earlier years). As solar has grown, it has become a bigger
driver of when power is cheap or expensive.

### Does it differ by season or hub?

```{r}
#| label: model-by-season
#| code-summary: "Code: effect by season"

no_uri |>
  group_by(season) |>
  group_modify(~ effect(lm(rt_price ~ renewable_share + hour_f + year_f, data = .x))) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = c(0, 2, 2, 3, 0), caption = "Effect by season")
```

```{r}
#| label: model-by-hub
#| code-summary: "Code: effect by hub"

ercot |>
  filter(!is.na(renewable_share)) |>
  filter(!(time_local >= as.POSIXct("2021-02-10", tz = "America/Chicago") &
           time_local <  as.POSIXct("2021-02-21", tz = "America/Chicago"))) |>
  mutate(hour_f  = factor(hour_local),
         month_f = factor(month(time_local)),
         year_f  = factor(year)) |>
  group_by(hub) |>
  group_modify(~ effect(lm(rt_price ~ renewable_share + hour_f + month_f + year_f, data = .x))) |>
  arrange(effect_per_10pp) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = c(0, 2, 2, 3, 0), caption = "Effect by hub")
```

**Findings:** Renewables lower prices most in summer, about \$23/MWh per
10-point increase, twice as much as in winter (\$10) or spring and fall (\$12).
Summer is when the grid is tightest, so extra wind and solar keep expensive
peaker plants switched off.

West Texas sees the biggest drop (\$16/MWh), compared with \$11–12 at the
other hubs. Most wind farms are in West Texas, and when power lines to the rest
of the state fill up, the extra power stays local and pushes West prices down
further. Houston, farthest from the wind farms, sees the smallest effect (\$11).

**A note on uncertainty:** the uncertainty numbers in these tables assume each
hour is independent, but neighboring hours are very similar (same weather, same
power plants running). That makes the true uncertainty larger than shown. The
conclusions don't change: the effects are far enough from zero that renewables
clearly lower prices, but the exact dollar amounts should be read as estimates.

## Takeaway

**Wind and solar lower Texas power prices, most of all when the grid is under
strain.**

- **Renewables are growing fast.** From 2021 to 2025, average solar output
  grew more than fourfold, passing nuclear and coal; wind grew about 20%.
- **They lower prices.** Each 10-point increase in wind and solar's share of
  demand cuts the real-time price by about \$12/MWh (\$9.50 day-ahead),
  comparing only similar hours and excluding Winter Storm Uri.
- **The effect is biggest when the grid is tight.** In summer the drop is
  about \$23/MWh, twice the winter effect. Prices stay low until the demand
  left for gas, coal and nuclear plants passes about 60,000 MW, then climb
  sharply, reaching a typical \$488/MWh in the rarest, tightest hours.
- **Prices peak in the evening, not when demand is highest.** As solar fades
  after sunset, other plants must fill the gap, so summer prices peak around
  8 p.m., three hours after peak demand.
- **Location matters.** West Texas, home to most wind farms, sees the largest
  drop (\$16/MWh). On very windy hours, power lines to the rest of the state
  fill up and West prices fall up to \$10 below the statewide price.
- **The effect tracks gas prices.** It was largest in 2022, when natural gas
  was expensive, and by 2025 renewables explained more than twice as much of
  the hour-to-hour price swings as in earlier years.
